cases.abstract: Asynchronous visual grasping can generate actions from queued older observations even while newer frames wait. We study observation-age-aware scheduling, which selects the latest completed camera frame at each action-generation start and discards older queued frames while retaining the serial controller's policy weights. Across four moving-object grasping tasks, we compare serial scheduling, a faster action decoder, and the proposed scheduler on the same GPU, using matched pretraining and task-demonstration data and 80 physical robot executions per task and method. Mean observation-to-command time falls from 96 ms with serial scheduling to 62 ms with the faster decoder and 41 ms with the scheduler; these measurements include waiting, preprocessing, and action generation but exclude command-to-motion time. Corresponding task-average success rates are 61%, 62%, and 74%. The scheduler drops 18% of arriving frames, trading observation retention for more timely commands and higher observed success on this workload. Because the evaluation changes multiple scheduling properties, it does not isolate observation freshness as the cause of these gains.
cases.results: Observation-age-aware scheduling reduced mean observation-to-command time to 41 ms, compared with 96 ms for serial scheduling and 62 ms for the faster decoder alone. This metric includes waiting, preprocessing, and action generation, not command-to-motion time. Task-average success was 74% with the scheduler, versus 61% and 62% for the respective comparators. These measurements cover four moving-object grasping tasks, with 80 physical executions per task and method on the same GPU and matched training data. The scheduler retained the serial policy weights but dropped 18% of arriving frames. The concurrent timing and task gains therefore describe the scheduling configuration as evaluated, rather than an isolated effect of observation freshness.

cases.abstract: Aggregate success can reverse the apparent ordering of navigation policies without any change in their behavior. We diagnose this sensitivity in a fixed-route warehouse evaluation by deriving weighted success rates and replaying the same recorded outputs under two aggregation rules. Policy U succeeds on 90% of short routes and 40% of long routes, whereas policy V achieves 75% and 70%, respectively. A dashboard weighting the two route families 9:1 reports 85% aggregate success for U and 74.5% for V. Equal task-family weighting instead yields 65% for U and 72.5% for V, reversing their ranking. The reversal reflects which route family the score emphasizes, not retraining or a new policy. We provide a report that places both task-family scores beside each aggregate, making the weighting dependence visible in the existing evaluation. The analysis establishes a limitation of aggregate-only comparisons on these fixed routes; it does not measure an improvement in deployed safety.
cases.results: Reaggregating the same recorded route outcomes changed the policy ranking. Under the dashboard's 9:1 short-to-long weighting, U scored 85% and V scored 74.5%; equal task-family weighting gave 65% and 72.5%, respectively. U's higher short-route success (90% versus 75%) explains its lead under the dashboard rule, while V's higher long-route success (70% versus 40%) produces the opposite ordering with equal weights. Neither policy's outputs changed, and no retraining was performed. Reporting both family-level scores alongside each aggregate exposes this dependence directly. These are descriptive comparisons of the fixed-route evaluation, not evidence of a new policy or improved deployed safety.

cases.abstract: Evaluating grasping from a fixed wrist-camera mount leaves transfer across mounting positions untested. We introduce a benchmark that records the same objects and manipulation tasks from six wrist-camera mounting positions, enabling evaluation of this viewpoint shift while keeping objects and task instructions shared. The released resource contains 2,400 demonstration episodes, with episode-disjoint training and validation data from three mounts and testing on three different mounts. An existing baseline trained on the training mounts achieves 84% success on validation mounts from that group but 57% on held-out mounts, exposing a performance gap under camera-mount transfer. Fine-tuning with 30 demonstrations from the held-out mounts raises success there to 72%, with model selection still using the original validation split. We release the benchmark and split definitions to support this evaluation. The protocol tests transfer across camera mounting positions rather than unseen objects, unseen tasks, new robots, or learning without training; the adaptation result additionally depends on target-mount demonstrations.
cases.results: The baseline achieved 84% success on validation data from the three training-group mounts and 57% on the three held-out mounts, a 27-percentage-point gap despite shared objects and task instructions. Training and validation episodes were disjoint, and the test mounts differed from those used for training. Fine-tuning with 30 demonstrations from the held-out mounts increased success there to 72%, recovering 15 percentage points while remaining below the original validation score. This adaptation used additional target-mount data, with model selection based on the original validation split. The results illustrate the benchmark's ability to expose sensitivity to camera mounting position and measure adaptation; they do not evaluate transfer to unseen objects, tasks, or robots.
